The SNARGs book generally treats multiple-path openings as a list of separate individual path openings. In section 29.2, it covers path-pruning. But I seem to recall from my time at RISC Zero that they didn't even do path pruning like the book describes, they instead did a different optimization where they topped out the Merkle tree at the height where there was expected to be one query. I guess this is not technically as efficient on average, but it has the benefit of being constant-time and more easily implementable in a circuit.

Which is all to say that path-pruning might not be too important, and I recommend we/I forego implementing it until and unless we know what precise proof system we want to model with it.
sounds good to me. if you could add this context into a comment in the file, that would be great

Path pruning is also done to reduce proof size (although it's not the only thing that matters for this) and, indeed, is not done by everyone at this point (see some data here: https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/1446.pdf). There might be incentives for most zkVMs to do this from the proof size point of view, which is that for L1 integration we'd like proofs which are <300kB. In this case, Risc Zero already has ~200kB proofs (dictated by the number of cycles that each proof accounts for) but I haven't checked the implementation details. Maybe topping out the Merkle tree is as effective or more in reducing the proof size, or maybe it's more or less irrelevant compared to capping the cycle count per proof to be aggregated.
